title: Badr Khan Beg Kurdish uprising crushed by Ottomans
summary: The first major 19th-century Kurdish uprising, led by Badr Khan Beg, was crushed by the Ottoman Empire. Subsequent uprisings were also suppressed, though the demand for Kurdish independence continued throughout the century.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: The first major 19th century Kurdish uprising, Badr Khan Beg, took place in 1847. The Ottomans crushed this and subsequent uprisings, but the demand for Kurdish independence continued throughout the rest of the century.

title: Iran's Constitutional Revolution begins
summary: Iran's 1906 Constitutional Revolution raised Kurdish hopes for autonomy, though the new constitution guaranteed many rights without explicitly protecting Kurdish ethnicity or culture.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In Iran, Kurdish dreams of autonomy after generations of Persian and Ottoman oppression started before World War I during Iran's 1906 Constitutional Revolution.

title: Young Turks forcibly deport 700,000 Kurds
summary: The Young Turks conducted a systematic ethnic cleansing, forcibly deporting 700,000 Kurds, with more than half dying during the brutal process.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: From 1916 to 1918 the Young Turks forcibly deported 700,000 Kurds, more than half of them dying during the brutal process.

title: Treaty of Sèvres signed, promising independent Kurdistan
summary: After World War I, the defeated Ottomans signed the Treaty of Sèvres, which split up the Ottoman Empire and included provisions for an independent Kurdistan.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: On August 10, 1920, after the conclusion of World War I, the defeated Ottomans were compelled to sign the Treaty of Sèvres.

title: Mustafa Kemal Ataturk wins War of Independence, abolishes sultanate
summary: The Turkish national movement, led by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, won the War of Independence and abolished the sultanate, forcing allied powers to renegotiate the Treaty of Sèvres.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: But in 1922 the Turkish national movement, led by Mustafa Kemal Ataturk, a vehement Turkish nationalist and military officer, won the War of Independence and abolished the sultanate.

title: Ataturk decrees 65 laws targeting Kurdish identity
summary: That same year as the Treaty of Lausanne, Ataturk decreed approximately 65 laws aimed at destroying Kurdish identity, including renaming Kurds 'Mountain Turks,' outlawing Kurdish language and celebrations, and confiscating Kurdish communal lands.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: That same year, Ataturk decreed some 65 laws aimed at destroying Kurdish identity: renaming them "Mountain Turks;" outlawing public use of the Kurdish language; making Kurdish celebrations illegal; forcibly changing Kurdish names of streets, villages, businesses, etc. to "proper Turkish" names; confiscating huge tracts of Kurdish communal lands; seizing Kurdish community funds; eliminating all Kurdish or Kurd-sympathetic organizations or political parties; and so on.

title: Treaty of Lausanne signed, eliminating Kurdish independence
summary: The Treaty of Lausanne, signed by Ataturk and his nationalist congress, replaced the Treaty of Sèvres and gave Kurdistan back to Turkey, failing to even recognize that the Kurds existed.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: The Treaty of Sèvres was scrapped, and a new treaty, the Treaty of Lausanne, was signed by Ataturk and his nationalist congress July 24, 1923. The Treaty of Lausanne gave Kurdistan back to Turkey, failing to even recognize that the Kurds existed.

title: Dozens of Kurdish newspapers and political organizations flourish in Iran
summary: By 1924, Kurds in Iran had developed dozens of newspapers, three radio stations, and half a dozen political parties, reflecting a period of civic and cultural flourishing between 1906 and 1925.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: By 1924, there were dozens of Kurdish newspapers, three radio stations, and half a dozen political parties.

title: Shah seizes power in Iran and begins Persianification campaign against Kurds
summary: In 1925, after oil was discovered in Iran, the Shah seized power with Western backing and launched a Persianification campaign targeting the Kurds and other minorities, resulting in mass displacements and suppression of Kurdish culture.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In 1925, after oil was discovered in the country, the Shah seized power with backing of the West (namely the UK and US). Though the Shah gave lip service to the constitution of 1906, he started a Persianification campaign against the numerous minorities inside Iran, including the Kurds.

title: Soviet Kurdish regional government unit disbanded under Stalin
summary: The special Soviet regional government unit set up to monitor Kurds was reorganized several times and ultimately dissolved in 1930 when the Stalinist central government feared it had grown too sympathetic to the Kurdish population.

citation.chapter: The Great Game: World Powers and the Kurds
citation.quote: This regional unit was reorganized several times and ultimately disbanded in 1930 when the Stalinist central government feared it had become too sympathetic to the Kurds.

title: Spanish Revolution as precedent for decentralized governance
summary: The Spanish Revolution of 1936 is cited as a past experiment in decentralized, non-state governance related to Rojava's democratic structures.

citation.chapter: Stateless Government: Radical Democracy and Decentralization
citation.quote: In the past two years, two-and-half million people in Rojava have been participating in this new form of governance, a governance related to that of the Spanish Revolution (1936), the Zapatistas (1994), the Argentine Neighborhood Assembly Movement (2001–2003), and Murray Bookchin's libertarian municipalism.

title: Syria gains independence from France, attacks Kurdish minority
summary: When Syria gained independence from France in 1946, the new Arab-controlled republic quickly attacked its 'internal enemies,' stripping approximately 200,000 Kurds of their identity papers and declaring them stateless.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: When Syria gained independence from France in 1946 it quickly attacked its "internal enemies." Close to 200,000 Kurds had their identity papers taken away and were declared stateless, allowing the new Syrian Republic to seize their land and property and to conscript them into forced labor.

title: Kurdish Democratic Party formed in Iraq
summary: In 1946, Iraqi Kurds formed the Kurdish Democratic Party as part of their ongoing political and military struggle against successive Iraqi regimes.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In 1946 they formed first the Kurdish Democratic Party and later, in 1975, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan.

title: Turkey joins NATO
summary: Turkey became a key member of NATO in 1952, a position it later used to lobby the alliance to designate the PKK and its sister organizations as terrorist groups.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: NATO, of which Turkey has been a key member since 1952, was lobbied heavily by Turkey in the 1990s to add the PKK and its sister organizations to the official terrorist watch-list, and in 2003 NATO conceded.

title: Ba'ath party comes to power in Iraq through military coups
summary: A series of military coups eventually elevated the Ba'ath party to power in Iraq in 1968, following British colonial rule and the establishment of the Kingdom of Iraq as a British puppet state.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: After putting down three unsuccessful but very bloody revolts, the British formally transferred control of Iraqi Kurdistan to the newly formed Kingdom of Iraq, which functioned as a British puppet state until a series of military coups eventually elevated the Ba'ath party to power in 1968.

title: Syria displaces 150,000 Kurds to create Arab corridor along Turkish border
summary: In 1973, Syrian officials decided to create an Arab corridor along the Turkish border and displaced about 150,000 Kurds without compensation.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In 1973, Syrian officials decided to create an Arab corridor along the Turkish border and displaced about 150,000 Kurds without compensation.

title: Turkey invades Cyprus; Greece retaliates by supporting Kurdish PKK
summary: Following Turkey's 1974 invasion of Cyprus, Greece supplied Kurds in Turkey and housed exiled PKK officials as a form of retaliation, though it later expelled the PKK after reaching a trade agreement with Turkey.

citation.chapter: The Great Game: World Powers and the Kurds
citation.quote: Greece supplied Kurds in Turkey and housed exiled PKK officials in order to punish Turkey for their 1974 invasion of Cyprus, but after coming to agreement on trade with Turkey they kicked the PKK out and stopped all aid.

title: Patriotic Union of Kurdistan founded in Iraq
summary: In 1975, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan was founded in Iraq as another major Kurdish political organization continuing the struggle for Kurdish rights.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In 1946 they formed first the Kurdish Democratic Party and later, in 1975, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan.

title: Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) founded in Istanbul
summary: In 1978, in a tea house in Istanbul, the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK) was founded — the first militant Kurdish resistance group to espouse explicitly Marxist ideology, calling for a communist Kurdistan.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In 1978, in a tea house in Istanbul, a new chapter in Kurdish resistance began with the founding of the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). The PKK was the first militant Kurdish resistance group to espouse explicitly Marxist ideology.

title: Saddam Hussein comes to power in Iraq
summary: Saddam Hussein came to power in Iraq in 1979, almost immediately entering into the decade-long Iran-Iraq war and bringing particular brutality down upon Iraqi Kurds.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: Eventually finding themselves in an uneasy truce with the Ba'ath party in the early 70s, Iraqi Kurds experienced a few brief years of relative calm before Saddam Hussein came to power in 1979.

title: Khomeini Revolution overthrows Shah in Iran
summary: The 1979 Khomeini Revolution overthrew the despotic Shah regime in Iran but did not improve life for the Kurds; the new fundamentalist regime accelerated nationalization and launched military assaults to wrest away Kurdish control of the north.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: The 1979 Khomeini Revolution overthrew the despotic Shah regime but did not improve the life of Kurds. The new fundamentalist regime accelerated the nationalization process with laws and actions targeted against the Kurds and their culture.

title: Turkey officially designates PKK a terrorist organization
summary: Turkey made its designation of the PKK as a terrorist organization official in 1979, a label it would later successfully export to NATO and Western governments.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: Turkey has always considered the PKK a terrorist organization, making it official in 1979.

title: Turkish military coup leads to arrest of PKK leadership
summary: In 1980, another Turkish military coup aimed to restore order led to the arrest of some PKK top leadership and the exile of most of the central committee to Syria and Western Europe.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In 1980, there was another Turkish military coup, aimed to restore order in the state. That year saw the arrest of some of the PKK top leadership and the exile of most of the central committee to Syria and Western Europe.

title: PKK launches full-scale guerrilla war in Turkey
summary: In 1984, after civilian rule was restored in Turkey and political prisoners were released, the PKK rebuilt its militant presence and launched a full-scale guerrilla war, mostly in southern Turkey.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In 1984, after civilian rule was restored in Turkey and a number of political prisoners were released, the PKK was again able to rebuild its militant presence in Turkey. The PKK launched a full-scale guerrilla war, mostly in the south of Turkey bust occasionally reaching as far north as Istanbul.

title: Bookchin's Ecology of Freedom made required reading for PKK militants
summary: Murray Bookchin's The Ecology of Freedom (1985) was designated required reading for all PKK militants by Öcalan, and went on to heavily influence the ideas put into practice in Rojava.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: It was Bookchin’s Ecology of Freedom (1985), however, which Öcalan made required reading for all PKK militants.

title: Al-Anfal Campaign massacres 100,000–200,000 Kurdish civilians
summary: During the al-Anfal Campaign, between 100,000 and 200,000 Kurdish civilians were massacred with chemical weapons and in concentration camps by Saddam Hussein's regime.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: In the al-Anfal Campaign of 1986–89 alone, between 100,000 and 200,000 Kurdish civilians were massacred with chemical weapons and in concentration camps.

title: Non-armed PKK support organizations formed in the USSR
summary: By 1986, non-armed PKK support organizations had covertly formed within the Soviet Union, operating illegally in the Transcaucasia region where the PKK had made inroads among the Kurdish population.

citation.chapter: The Great Game: World Powers and the Kurds
citation.quote: By 1986, non-armed PKK support organizations had formed in the USSR, though they were technically illegal.

title: US silent as Saddam Hussein gasses Kurdish populations
summary: From 1987 until Iraq's invasion of Kuwait, the US said nothing and at times even supported Iraq in the UN while Saddam Hussein was gassing tens of thousands of Kurds and bombing Kurdish towns and villages.

citation.chapter: The Great Game: World Powers and the Kurds
citation.quote: Yet from 1987 until the Iraqi invasion of Kuwait, the US said nothing. At times, the US even supported Iraq in the UN, when Saddam Hussein was gassing tens of thousands of Kurds and bombing whole Kurdish towns and villages.

title: United States and NATO allies first invade Iraq
summary: Iraq was first invaded by the United States and its NATO allies in 1990, a conflict the Kurds used to leverage political advantage.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: it was invaded by the United States and its NATO allies first in 1990 and then again in 2003.

title: Iraq occupies Kuwait; US declares Kurds "natural allies"
summary: When Iraq occupied Kuwait in August 1990, Saddam Hussein became America's foremost enemy and President George Bush Sr. publicly declared Kurds to be the US's "natural allies," urging them to revolt against the Baghdad regime.

citation.chapter: The Great Game: World Powers and the Kurds
citation.quote: During the first Gulf War, when Iraq occupied the oil-rich emirate of Kuwait in August 1990, Saddam Hussein became America's enemy number one.

title: Kurdistan Regional Government established in Iraq
summary: The Kurds leveraged the 1990 US-led invasion of Iraq to establish the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) in 1991.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: The Kurds would use both of these conflicts to leverage as much advantage as possible, which ultimately led to the establishment of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) in 1991 and its de jure independence in 2005.

title: Zapatista movement as precedent for stateless governance
summary: The Zapatista movement of 1994 is cited alongside the Spanish Revolution as a past experiment in decentralized, non-state governance related to Rojava.

citation.chapter: Stateless Government: Radical Democracy and Decentralization
citation.quote: In the past two years, two-and-half million people in Rojava have been participating in this new form of governance, a governance related to that of the Spanish Revolution (1936), the Zapatistas (1994), the Argentine Neighborhood Assembly Movement (2001–2003), and Murray Bookchin's libertarian municipalism.

title: Zapatista uprising begins in Chiapas, Mexico
summary: The Zapatistas launched their insurrection in the Lacandon Jungle of Chiapas, declaring autonomy and introducing Zapatismo — a leftist configuration rejecting hierarchy, party control, and state-building — inspiring the global progressive Left.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: Thousands of miles away, on January 1, 1994 (five years before Öcalan’s capture) a new type of liberation struggle kicked off in the forgotten mountain jungles of Chiapas, Mexico.

title: Öcalan arrested in Nairobi and imprisoned in Turkey
summary: PKK leader Abdullah Öcalan was captured by Turkish military intelligence in Nairobi, flown back to Turkey, and held as the sole prisoner on a prison island, triggering an ideological crisis within the PKK.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: For the PKK, the crisis in their communist faith didn’t occur until 1999 when their leader Öcalan was arrested in Nairobi by the MIT (Turkish military intelligence), flown back to Turkey, and incarcerated on a prison island upon which he was the only inmate.

title: Öcalan writes The Roots of Civilization from prison
summary: Drawing on Bookchin's anarchist philosophy, Öcalan wrote The Roots of Civilization (2001) from inside his island prison, applying Bookchin's ideas to the Kurdish question.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: From inside prison, Öcalan absorbed Bookchin’s ideas (most notably Bookchin’s Civilization Narratives: The Ecology of Freedom and Urbanization Against Cities) and wrote his own book based on these ideas, The Roots of Civilization (2001).

title: Argentine Neighborhood Assembly Movement
summary: The Argentine Neighborhood Assembly Movement of 2001–2003 is cited as a past experiment in decentralized, participatory governance related to Rojava's council system.

citation.chapter: Stateless Government: Radical Democracy and Decentralization
citation.quote: In the past two years, two-and-half million people in Rojava have been participating in this new form of governance, a governance related to that of the Spanish Revolution (1936), the Zapatistas (1994), the Argentine Neighborhood Assembly Movement (2001–2003), and Murray Bookchin's libertarian municipalism.

title: EU and US add PKK to terrorist lists
summary: The year before NATO's 2003 concession, both the EU and the US added the PKK to their terrorist lists, where the organization remains to this day.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: The year before, both the EU and the US added the PKK to their terrorist lists, where they remain to this day.

title: United States and NATO allies invade Iraq a second time
summary: Iraq was invaded again by the United States and its NATO allies in 2003, a conflict the Kurds again leveraged for political advantage, contributing to the KRG's de jure independence in 2005.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: it was invaded by the United States and its NATO allies first in 1990 and then again in 2003. The Kurds would use both of these conflicts to leverage as much advantage as possible, which ultimately led to the establishment of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) in 1991 and its de jure independence in 2005.

title: NATO adds PKK to official terrorist watch-list
summary: In 2003, following heavy lobbying by Turkey throughout the 1990s, NATO conceded and added the PKK and its sister organizations to its official terrorist watch-list.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: NATO, of which Turkey has been a key member since 1952, was lobbied heavily by Turkey in the 1990s to add the PKK and its sister organizations to the official terrorist watch-list, and in 2003 NATO conceded.

title: ISIS begins building forces following American invasion of Iraq
summary: ISIS, formerly an offshoot of Al-Qaeda in Iraq, began building its forces following the American invasion of Iraq in 2003, gaining military experience fighting NATO forces in Fallujah during the initial years of the Coalition Occupation.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: ISIS did not burst recently onto the scene in a simplistic blitzkrieg of hardline puritanical Sunni ideology — it has been building its forces since the American invasion of Iraq in 2003. Formerly an offshoot of Al-Qaeda in Iraq, ISIS gained valuable military experience fighting NATO forces in Fallujah during the initial years of the Coalition Occupation of Iraq, eventually rebranding itself the Islamic State of Iraq.

title: PKK organization reported in Kazakhstan
summary: According to Turkish press reports, a PKK organization was operating in Kazakhstan in 2004, indicating the continued reach of PKK networks in the former Soviet space.

citation.chapter: The Great Game: World Powers and the Kurds
citation.quote: According to Turkish press, there was even a PKK organization in Kazakhstan in 2004.

title: Öcalan attempts to arrange a meeting with Murray Bookchin
summary: In 2004, Öcalan reached out through his lawyers to request a meeting with Bookchin, calling himself Bookchin's student and wishing to discuss his new manuscript In Defense of People.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: In 2004, Öcalan tried to arrange a meeting with Bookchin through his lawyers, describing himself as Bookchin’s “student” and eager to adapt Bookchin’s ideas to the Kurdish question.

title: Öcalan writes In Defense of People
summary: From prison in 2004, Öcalan completed In Defense of People, a manuscript he hoped would shift the discourse of the Kurdish struggle toward democratic confederalism.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: In particular, Öcalan wanted to discuss his newest manuscript, In Defense of People (2004), which he had hoped would change the discourse of the Kurdish struggle.

title: Kurdistan Regional Government achieves de jure independence
summary: The Kurdistan Regional Government achieved de jure independence in 2005, a result of the Kurds leveraging both the 1990 and 2003 US-led invasions of Iraq.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: The Kurds would use both of these conflicts to leverage as much advantage as possible, which ultimately led to the establishment of the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) in 1991 and its de jure independence in 2005.

title: PKK adopts democratic confederalism at people's congress
summary: At a people's congress on May 17, 2005, the PKK officially adopted democratic confederalism as their platform, rejecting state-building in favor of a decentralized, self-sufficient model of governance.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: the PKK had adopted as their official platform in a people’s congress on May 17th, 2005.

title: Murray Bookchin dies of congestive heart failure
summary: Murray Bookchin, whose anarchist ecological philosophy had profoundly shaped the PKK's ideological shift, died of congestive heart failure in 2006 at age 85.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: Murray Bookchin died of congested heart failure two years later, in 2006.

title: PKK congress honors Bookchin and vows to implement democratic confederalism
summary: A PKK congress held in 2006 honored Murray Bookchin as one of the greatest social scientists of the 20th century and pledged to implement his thesis on state, power, and hierarchy through their struggle.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: A PKK congress held later that year hailed the American thinker as “one of the greatest social scientists of the 20th century,” and vowed that “Bookchin’s thesis on the state, power, and hierarchy will be implemented and realized through our struggle…. We will put this promise into practice, this as the first society that establishes a tangible democratic confederalism.”

title: PKK begins democratic confederalism experiments in Turkish villages
summary: From 2009 onward, the PKK began implementing democratic confederalism in scattered villages along the Turkey-Iraq border, experiments that would serve as an inspiration for the broader Rojava revolution.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: The PKK has attempted (and succeeded to some degree) to implement democratic confederalism in scattered villages in Turkey along the Iraq border since 2009, experiments that served as an inspiration for much of the Rojava revolution.

title: Rojava provides over 40% of Syria's GNP despite hosting 17% of its population
summary: In 2010, a year before the Arab Spring reached Syria, the Rojava region contributed more than 40% of the country's GNP and 70% of its exports, yet its residents earned well below the national median income.

citation.chapter: A People's Economy
citation.quote: In 2010, a year before the Arab Spring exploded in Syria, the Rojava region provided over 40% of the country's GNP and 70% of its exports despite only about 17% of Syria's population living in the region.

title: Syrian civil war begins as part of the Arab Spring uprisings
summary: The Syrian civil war emerged from the broader Arab Spring protests of spring 2011, with Kurds joining students, workers, and others demanding an end to Assad's repressive dictatorship.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: The Syrian civil war began as part of the general uprisings in spring 2011 in North Africa and the Middle East that the West dubbed the “Arab Spring.”

title: Syrian protests turn into armed insurrection against Assad regime
summary: By autumn 2011, the largely peaceful Arab Spring demonstrations in Syria had transformed into a full armed insurrection against the Assad dictatorship after the government sent in troops to crush the movement.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: By autumn, the mostly peaceful protests that had taken place in the spring had morphed into a full-on armed insurrection against the Assad regime.

title: Assad grants citizenship to 200,000 stateless Kurds
summary: As protests began, the Syrian government granted citizenship to an estimated 200,000 stateless Kurds in an attempt to neutralize potential Kurdish opposition to the Assad regime.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: When the protests first began, Assad’s government finally granted citizenship to an estimated 200,000 stateless Kurds in an effort to neutralize potential Kurdish opposition.

title: Supreme Kurdish Council (SKC) formed in Rojava
summary: In early 2012, with tensions between the PYD and KRG-aligned Kurdish parties threatening to turn violent, KRG President Massoud Barzani and PKK leaders brokered the formation of the Supreme Kurdish Council, a coalition of over fifteen political parties and hundreds of community councils.

citation.chapter: From Red Star to Ishtar’s Star: Departing from authoritarian communism
citation.quote: In early 2012, when it looked like the tension between the two groups might result in armed conflict, the President of the KRG Massoud Barzani and leaders of the PKK brought the two groups together to form a new coalition called the Supreme Kurdish Council (SKC) made up of over fifteen political parties and hundreds of community councils.

title: PYD launches the Social Economy Plan in Rojava
summary: In 2012, the PYD launched what it originally called the Social Economy Plan, which would later be renamed the People's Economy Plan (PEP), drawing on the writings of Öcalan and the lived experiences of Kurds in North Kurdistan.

citation.chapter: A People's Economy
citation.quote: In 2012, the PYD launched what it originally called the Social Economy Plan, which would later be renamed the People's Economy Plan (PEP). The PEP was based on the writings of Öcalan and the lived experiences of Kurds in North Kurdistan (southern Turkey).

title: Traditional private property abolished in Rojava
summary: In late 2012, the Rojava councils abolished traditional private property, placing all buildings, land, and infrastructure under council control and instituting an 'ownership by use' principle that prevented speculation and capital accumulation.

citation.chapter: A People's Economy
citation.quote: Traditional "private property" was abolished in late 2012, meaning all buildings, land, and infrastructure fell under control of the various city councils.

title: Ceasefire declared in PKK conflict with Turkey
summary: A ceasefire was declared in 2013, ending a conflict between the PKK and Turkey that had lasted from 1984 and cost tens of thousands of lives, including a great many Kurdish civilians.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: Tens of thousands of people in Turkey, including a great many civilians (90% of them Kurdish), lost their lives in this conflict, which lasted until a ceasefire was declared in 2013.

title: ISIS declares itself the only legitimate Islamic Caliphate
summary: In mid-2014, the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) declared itself the only legitimate Islamic Caliphate and renamed itself simply the Islamic State (IS), having seized large swathes of territory across Eastern Syria and Western Iraq.

citation.chapter: The History and Context of the Rojava Revolution
citation.quote: The Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS) declared itself to be the only legitimate Islamic Caliphate in mid-2014, going so far as to rename itself simply the Islamic State (IS).

title: Rojava regional council overruled by three local assemblies on weapons policy
summary: In August 2014, a regional council in Rojava decided local security forces could carry weapons while patrolling a city, but three local assemblies rejected the decision, demonstrating the primacy of local councils over upper councils.

citation.chapter: Stateless Government: Radical Democracy and Decentralization
citation.quote: In August 2014, for example, a regional council decided that local security forces could carry weapons while patrolling a city, but three local assemblies did not approve this decision, so in those local assembly areas security must refrain from carrying weapons.

title: Rojava representatives tour Europe seeking trading partners
summary: In autumn 2014, representatives of Rojava travelled around Europe looking to create trading partners, apparently proposing standard free-market trade arrangements even as financial institutions were being eliminated inside Rojava.

citation.chapter: A People's Economy
citation.quote: In Autumn, 2014, representatives of Rojava travelled around Europe looking to create "trading partners" and seemed to be suggesting a standard free market policy, while at the same time eliminating banks and other financial institutions inside Rojava.
